categories: Brackets and Braces, and order of operations
levels: Level 1: ideas and stories, almost no numbers
Level 3: brackets, first algebra and shapes
Level 4: algebra, geometry and chance in depth

articles.t: What is an unknown? Algebra and the balance scales
k: In algebra, a letter such as x stands for a number we do not know yet.
An equation is like a balance: both sides weigh the same.
3x means 3 times x; mathematicians leave out the times sign.

q.q: If x plus 4 equals 10, what is x?
q.ex: Take 4 from both sides of the balance: x equals 6.

articles.t: Solving equations: doing the same to both sides
k: To solve an equation, undo what has been done to x, in reverse order.
Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.
Unknowns on both sides: gather the x terms on one side first.

q.q: Solve 3x plus 2 equals x plus 10.
q.ex: Take x from both sides: 2x plus 2 equals 10. Take 2: 2x equals 8. So x equals 4.

k: A graph is a picture of a rule: each point pairs an input x with an output y.
A straight line has the form y equals m x plus c, where m is the steepness and c is where it crosses the vertical axis.
Steepness, or gradient, means how much y goes up for each step of 1 in x.

q.q: In y equals 2x plus 1, how steep is the line?
q.ex: The number in front of x, here 2, is the gradient: up 2 for every step of 1 to the right.

k: A function is a rule that turns each input into exactly one output, like a machine.
f of x means the output of machine f when x is put in.
Machines can be chained together, and some can be run backwards: that is the inverse function.

q.q: If f of x equals x squared plus 1, what is f of 3?
q.ex: Three squared is 9, plus 1 is 10.

k: A quadratic equation has an x squared term, such as x squared plus 5x plus 6 equals 0.
If two brackets multiply to zero, one of them must be zero.
The quadratic formula solves any quadratic: x equals minus b plus or minus the square root of b squared minus 4ac, all over 2a.

q.q: Solve open bracket x minus 2 close bracket open bracket x minus 7 close bracket equals 0.
q.ex: If the product is zero, one bracket is zero: x minus 2 is 0 or x minus 7 is 0.

articles.t: Infinity: Hilbert's hotel and bigger infinities
k: Infinity is not a number you reach, but the idea of going on forever.
Two sets are the same size if their members can be paired off one to one.
Cantor proved that some infinities are bigger than others: there are more decimals than whole numbers.

q.q: Hilbert's hotel is full, with infinitely many rooms. Can it take one more guest?
o: Yes, everyone moves up one room
q.ex: Move each guest from room n to room n plus 1, and room 1 becomes free.

articles.t: Prime numbers: the atoms of arithmetic
k: A prime number has exactly two factors, 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 and so on.
Every whole number above 1 can be built from primes in exactly one way.
Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes.

q.q: Which of these is a prime number?
q.ex: 21 is 3 times 7, and 27 is 3 times 9, but 29 has no factors except 1 and itself.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 1: What grouping means
k: Brackets group things together so the group is treated as one thing.
Brackets come in pairs: an opening bracket and a closing bracket.
In this app, an opening bracket rises in pitch and a closing bracket falls.

q.q: What is the main job of a pair of brackets?
o: To group things so they are treated as one
To show a number is negative
q.ex: Brackets group. Whatever is inside is treated as a single thing.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 2: Order of operations, BIDMAS and BODMAS, with stories
k: BIDMAS: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction.
Multiplication and division are equal partners, done left to right; so are addition and subtraction.
Without brackets, 2 plus 3 times 4 is 14, because multiplying comes before adding.

q.q: What is 2 plus 3 times 4?
q.ex: Multiplication comes before addition: 3 times 4 is 12, plus 2 is 14.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 3: Round brackets at work
k: A number written right next to a bracket means multiply: 3 brackets x plus 1 means 3 times the bracket.
Round brackets can hold a negative number, keeping its minus sign attached: minus 3, squared, is 9.
f of x is written f, open bracket, x, close bracket, and is not a multiplication.

q.q: What is open bracket minus 3 close bracket, squared?
q.ex: The whole bracket is squared: minus 3 times minus 3 is plus 9.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 4: Square brackets, curly braces and nesting
k: When brackets sit inside brackets, they are nested. Work from the innermost outwards.
Square brackets and curly braces are often used as outer layers, so the eye can match pairs easily.
In this app, deeper brackets sound higher, and square and curly ones have their own timbres.

q.q: In nested brackets, where do you start?
q.ex: Work from the inside out, like opening Russian dolls in reverse.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 5: Curly braces for sets
k: Curly braces hold a set: a collection of things, listed between the braces.
In a set, order does not matter and nothing is counted twice.
Set-builder notation describes a set by a rule: the set of x such that x is greater than zero.

q.q: Is the set 1, 2, 3 the same as the set 3, 2, 1?
o: Yes, order does not matter in a set
Only if they are written in square brackets
q.ex: A set only cares what is in it, not the order.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 6: Brackets in algebra: expanding
k: Expanding means multiplying out a bracket: 3 brackets x plus 2 becomes 3x plus 6.
The number outside multiplies every term inside, not just the first.
Two brackets multiplied together: multiply each term in the first by each term in the second.

q.q: What is 4 brackets x plus 3, expanded?
q.ex: The 4 multiplies both terms: 4 times x and 4 times 3.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 7: Brackets in algebra: factorising
k: Factorising is expanding in reverse: putting things back into brackets.
Look for a common factor, something that divides every term, and take it outside the bracket.
To factorise x squared plus 5x plus 6, find two numbers that add to 5 and multiply to 6: 2 and 3.

q.q: What is 6x plus 9, factorised?
q.ex: 3 divides both 6x and 9, so take 3 outside: 3, open bracket, 2x plus 3, close bracket.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 8: Interval notation: square for in, round for out
k: An interval is a stretch of the number line between two end points.
A square bracket means the end point is included; a round bracket means it is left out.
Infinity always takes a round bracket, because you can never reach it.

q.q: Does the interval open square bracket 0, 1, close round bracket include the number 1?
q.ex: The round bracket at the 1 end means 1 is left out. The square bracket at 0 means 0 is included.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 9: Common confusions, and how to avoid them
k: Open bracket a plus b close bracket squared is not a squared plus b squared; it has a middle term 2ab.
A minus sign in front of a bracket flips every sign inside.
Brackets can mean grouping, multiplying, a function, a point, or an interval: the context tells you which.

q.q: What does open bracket x plus 3 close bracket squared expand to?
q.ex: Multiply the bracket by itself: x squared, plus 3x, plus 3x, plus 9.

articles.t: Brackets and Braces, part 10: Review and practice
k: Brackets group; work out the innermost first.
BIDMAS: brackets, indices, then division and multiplication, then addition and subtraction.
Curly braces hold sets; square for in and round for out in intervals.

q.q: What is 3 plus open bracket 2 times 4 close bracket squared?
q.ex: Bracket first: 8. Then the power: 64. Then 3 plus 64 is 67.

q.q: Which of these is the empty set?
o: Open curly brace, zero, close curly brace
Open curly brace, close curly brace
q.ex: The empty set has nothing between its braces. The set containing zero has one element, zero.

articles.t: Calculus, part 1: Limits, or getting closer and closer
k: Calculus is the mathematics of change and of adding up infinitely many tiny pieces.
A limit is the value something gets closer and closer to, even if it never quite arrives.
One half plus one quarter plus one eighth, and so on forever, has the limit 1.

q.q: What is the limit of one half plus one quarter plus one eighth, and so on forever?
q.ex: Each step covers half of the remaining gap to 1, so the total gets as close to 1 as you like.

articles.t: Calculus, part 2: Derivatives, or speed and slope
k: A derivative measures how fast something is changing at one instant.
It is the limit of average speeds over shorter and shorter times.
The derivative of x squared is 2x: the steepness of the curve y equals x squared is 2x.

q.q: If y equals x squared, what is the rate of change, d y by d x, when x is 3?
q.ex: The derivative of x squared is 2x, and 2 times 3 is 6.

articles.t: Calculus, part 3: Integrals, or adding up slices
k: An integral adds up infinitely many infinitely thin slices.
The integral of a speed over time gives the total distance travelled.
The long S sign of the integral comes from the word summa, meaning sum.

q.q: You travel at a steady 30 miles an hour for 2 hours. What does the integral of your speed over that time give?
q.ex: Integrating speed over time gives the distance: 30 times 2 is 60 miles.

articles.t: Calculus, part 4: The fundamental theorem, two sides of one coin
k: The fundamental theorem of calculus says that integrating and differentiating undo each other.
To find an integral, find a function whose derivative is the thing being integrated.
The integral from 0 to 3 of x squared is 9, because x cubed over 3 has derivative x squared.

q.q: Why is the fundamental theorem so useful?
o: It lets us find areas by running derivatives backwards
q.ex: Instead of adding infinitely many slices, we find a function whose derivative is our curve.

articles.t: Calculus, part 5: Differential equations in plain words
k: A differential equation is a rule about how something changes, written with derivatives.
When the rate of growth is proportional to the size, the result is exponential growth.
Newton's laws of motion and most of physics are written as differential equations.

q.q: A population grows at a rate proportional to its size. What kind of growth is that?
q.ex: Growth proportional to size is exponential growth: the bigger it gets, the faster it grows.

articles.t: Shapes in words: points, lines and angles
k: An angle measures an amount of turn; a full turn is 360 degrees, a right angle is 90.
The angles inside any triangle add up to 180 degrees.
A polygon with n sides has angles adding to n minus 2, times 180 degrees.

q.q: What do the three angles of any triangle add up to?
q.ex: Always 180 degrees, a straight line's worth of turning.

k: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the longest side equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.
A squared plus b squared equals c squared, where c is the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle.
The 3, 4, 5 triangle is the simplest whole-number example: 9 plus 16 is 25.

q.q: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 6 and 8. How long is the longest side?
q.ex: 6 squared is 36, 8 squared is 64, together 100, and the square root of 100 is 10.

k: Pi is the distance around any circle divided by the distance across it, about 3.14159.
Circumference equals pi times diameter; area equals pi times radius squared.
Pi is irrational: its decimal digits go on forever without repeating.

q.q: A circle has a diameter of 10 centimetres. Roughly how far is it around?
q.ex: Circumference is pi times diameter: about 3.14 times 10, which is about 31.4.

articles.t: Trigonometry: SOH CAH TOA in words
k: Trigonometry links the angles of a right-angled triangle to the ratios of its sides.
SOH CAH TOA: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent is opposite over adjacent.
Sine and cosine also describe waves and anything that goes round in circles.

q.q: In SOH CAH TOA, what is tangent?
q.ex: TOA: tangent equals opposite over adjacent.

articles.t: Before numbers: tally sticks, clay tokens and the Babylonians
k: The earliest counting was matching: one notch for one thing.
Clay tokens in Mesopotamia led to writing and to written numbers.
The Babylonians counted in sixties, which is why an hour has sixty minutes.

q.q: Why does an hour have sixty minutes?
o: Because the Babylonians counted in sixties
Because sixty is a prime number
q.ex: The Babylonians used base sixty, and their astronomy passed it down to our clocks and angles.

articles.t: The journey of zero: from Babylon to India, Baghdad and Pisa
k: Zero began as a placeholder for an empty column and became a number in India.
Brahmagupta, in 628, gave the first rules for calculating with zero.
Al-Khwarizmi and Fibonacci carried Indian numerals to the Islamic world and to Europe.

q.q: Who wrote the first known rules for doing arithmetic with zero, in the year 628?
q.ex: The Indian astronomer Brahmagupta wrote rules such as: a number plus zero is that same number.

articles.t: What is a proof? Certainty in mathematics
k: A proof is a chain of reasoning showing that something must be true in every case.
Checking examples is not proof; one counter-example is enough to disprove a claim.
Proof by contradiction: assume the opposite, and show it leads to nonsense.

q.q: How many examples does it take to disprove a claim that something is always true?
q.ex: A single counter-example is enough to show a claim is not always true.

articles.t: Logic words: and, or, not, if and then
k: In logic, or usually means one or the other or both.
If A then B does not mean if B then A: that mistake is called affirming the consequent.
The contrapositive, if not B then not A, means exactly the same as if A then B.

q.q: All cats are mammals. Rex is a mammal. Does it follow that Rex is a cat?
q.ex: No. All cats are mammals, but not all mammals are cats. Rex could be a dog.

articles.t: Mental arithmetic: making friends with ten
k: Number bonds to ten, such as 7 and 3, are the foundation of mental adding.
Bridging through ten: to add 8 and 5, take 2 from the 5 to make 10, then add the 3 left over.
Compensation: to add 99, add 100 and take 1 away.

q.q: What is 47 plus 99, using the add a hundred trick?
q.ex: Add 100 to get 147, then take away 1 to get 146.

articles.t: Times tables by pattern, and multiplying in your head
k: Multiplication is repeated adding: 4 times 3 is three lots of four.
Order does not matter: 7 times 8 is the same as 8 times 7, which halves the tables to learn.
To multiply bigger numbers, split them: 23 times 4 is 20 times 4 plus 3 times 4.

q.q: What is 9 times 7, using the nine times table pattern?
q.ex: Ten sevens are seventy, take away one seven: sixty-three.

articles.t: Estimating: the art of being roughly right
k: Estimating means rounding to friendly numbers to get a quick rough answer.
An estimate is the best check on a calculator: it catches answers ten times too big.
Orders of magnitude describe size in powers of ten: tens, hundreds, thousands, millions.

q.q: Roughly what is 49 times 21?
q.ex: Fifty times twenty is a thousand, so the answer is about a thousand. In fact it is 1,029.

articles.t: Place value: why the position of a digit matters
k: In our base ten system, each place is worth ten times the place to its right.
Zero holds an empty place, so 305 is not 35.
Saying a number aloud already describes its place values: three hundred and five.

q.q: In the number 4,072, what is the 7 worth?
q.ex: The 7 is in the tens place, so it is worth seven tens, which is seventy.

articles.t: Negative numbers: debts, temperatures and the number line
k: Negative numbers are numbers below zero, like debts or frosty temperatures.
On the number line, adding moves you up or right, subtracting moves you down or left.
Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding: taking away a debt makes you richer.

q.q: What is 3 minus 5?
q.ex: Start at 3 and step down 5: you pass zero and land on minus 2.

articles.t: Fractions by ear: halves, quarters and slices of cake
k: A fraction is a number of equal parts: the bottom number says how many parts make a whole, the top says how many we have.
Equivalent fractions are the same amount cut differently: one half equals two quarters.
To add fractions, first cut them into the same size of piece.

q.q: Which is larger, one third or one quarter?
q.ex: Cut a cake into three and each slice is bigger than when it is cut into four.

articles.t: Decimals, percentages and ratios: three ways to say the same thing
k: Decimals continue place value to the right: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
Per cent means out of a hundred: fifty per cent is one half, twenty-five per cent is one quarter.
A ratio compares amounts: two to three means two parts of one thing for every three of another.

q.q: What is 10 per cent of 250?
q.ex: Ten per cent is one tenth, and one tenth of 250 is 25.

articles.t: Welcome to Maths by Ear: learning mathematics by listening
k: Mathematics is ideas before it is symbols, and ideas can be heard.
Every formula in this app is said once in words, then explained in plain English.
Short tones mark brackets: opening tones rise, closing tones fall.

q.q: In this app, what does a falling tone after a bracket mean?
q.ex: Opening tones rise and closing tones fall, like a door swinging open and then shutting.

articles.t: Invented or discovered? A gentle tour of the philosophy of mathematics
k: Platonists think mathematical objects exist independently and are discovered.
Formalists think mathematics is a game of symbols and rules that we invent.
Intuitionists think mathematics is built in the human mind, step by step.

q.q: Which view says numbers exist on their own, outside space and time, waiting to be discovered?
q.ex: Platonism, named after Plato, holds that mathematical objects are real and timeless, and we discover them.

articles.t: Gödel's incompleteness theorems in plain words
k: Gödel showed that any consistent rulebook for arithmetic leaves some true statements unprovable.
His trick was a sentence that says, in effect, this sentence cannot be proved.
A consistent system of this kind cannot prove its own consistency.

q.q: What did Gödel show about a consistent set of rules strong enough for arithmetic?
o: It can prove every true statement
Some true statements cannot be proved within it
q.ex: Gödel's first incompleteness theorem: there are always true statements the rules cannot prove.

articles.t: Chance: coins, dice and the language of probability
k: Probability measures how likely something is, from 0 for impossible to 1 for certain.
For equally likely outcomes, probability is favourable outcomes divided by all outcomes.
Coins have no memory: after five heads, the next toss is still a fifty-fifty chance.

q.q: What is the probability of rolling a six on a fair die?
q.ex: There are six equally likely faces and one of them is a six.

articles.t: Averages and spread: mean, median and mode
k: The mean adds everything up and shares it out equally.
The median is the middle value when everything is lined up in order; it is not pulled around by extremes.
Spread, such as the range or standard deviation, says how far values scatter from the average.

q.q: Five people earn 20, 22, 25, 28 and 500 thousand pounds. Which average best describes a typical person?
q.ex: The median, 25 thousand, is not dragged upward by the one huge salary. The mean is 119 thousand, which describes nobody.

k: Philosophy of mathematics is the branch of philosophy that deals with the nature of mathematics and its relationship to other areas of philosophy, particularly epistemology and metaphysics.
Mathematical Platonism is the form of realism that suggests that mathematical entities, such as numbers, are abstract, have no spatiotemporal or causal properties, and are eternal and unchanging.

In philosophy of mathematics, formalism is the view that holds that statements of mathematics and logic can be considered to be statements about the consequences of the manipulation of strings (alphan
In philosophy of mathematics, intuitionism, or neointuitionism (opposed to preintuitionism), is an approach where mathematics is considered to be purely the result of the constructive mental activity

In philosophy of mathematics, logicism is a school of thought comprising one or more of the theses that—for some coherent meaning of 'logic'—mathematics is an extension of logic, some or all of mathem

articles.t: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences
k: "The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences" was the title of the 1959 Richard Courant Lecture in Mathematical Sciences, delivered at New York University by the physicist Eu
Mathematical beauty is a type of aesthetic value that is experienced in doing or contemplating mathematics.

Foundations of mathematics are the logical and mathematical frameworks that allow the development of mathematics without generating self-contradictory theories, and to have reliable concepts of theorems, proofs, algorithms, and so on in particular.

In mathematics, Hilbert's program, formulated by German mathematician David Hilbert in the early 1920s, was a proposed solution to the foundational crisis of mathematics, when early attempts to clarif

Mathematical anxiety, also known as math phobia and math anxiety, is a feeling of tension and anxiety that interferes with the manipulation of numbers and the solving of mathematical problems in daily life and academic situations.
Numerical cognition is a subdiscipline of cognitive science that studies the cognitive, developmental and neural bases of numbers and mathematics.
In mathematics education, ethnomathematics is the study of the relationship between mathematics and culture.
Mathematics is a field of knowledge concerned with abstract concepts such as numbers, geometric shapes, sets, functions, and probabilities.
The history of mathematics deals with the origin of discoveries in mathematics and the mathematical methods and notation of the past.

Babylonian mathematics (also known as Assyro-Babylonian mathematics) is the mathematics developed or practiced by the people of Mesopotamia, as attested by sources surviving mainly from the Old Babylo

Ancient Egyptian mathematics is the mathematics that was developed and used in Ancient Egypt around 3000 to around 300 BC, from the Old Kingdom of Egypt until roughly the beginning of Hellenistic Egypt.
Ancient Greek mathematics refers to the history of mathematical ideas and texts in Ancient Greece during classical and late antiquity, mostly from the 5th century BC to the 6th century AD.
The tradition of Indian mathematics flourished in South Asia from circa 1200 BC until the late 18th century, when it merged into a global discipline.
Mathematics emerged independently in China by the 11th century BC.

articles.t: Mathematics in the medieval Islamic world
k: Mathematics during the Golden Age of Islam, especially during the 9th and 10th centuries, was built upon syntheses of Greek mathematics (Euclid, Archimedes, Apollonius) and Indian mathematics (Aryabhata, Brahmagupta).
The Mayan numeral system was the system to represent numbers and calendar dates in the Maya civilization.

The history of mathematical notation covers the introduction, development, and cultural diffusion of mathematical symbols and the conflicts between notational methods that arise during a notation's move to popularity or obsolescence.
Algebra can essentially be considered as doing computations similar to those of arithmetic but with non-numerical mathematical objects.
Geometry (geo- "earth", -metron "measurement") arose as the field of knowledge dealing with spatial relationships.
Early study of triangles can be traced to Egyptian mathematics (Rhind Mathematical Papyrus) and Babylonian mathematics during the 2nd millennium BC.
Calculus, originally called infinitesimal calculus, is a mathematical discipline focused on limits, continuity, derivatives, integrals, and infinite series.
Statistics, in the modern sense of the word, began evolving in the 18th century in response to the novel needs of industrializing sovereign states.

Probability has a dual aspect: on the one hand the likelihood of hypotheses given the evidence for them, and on the other hand the behavior of stochastic processes such as the throwing of dice or coins.
The Elements is a mathematical treatise written around 300 BC by the Ancient Greek mathematician Euclid.
The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus (RMP; also designated as papyrus British Museum 10057, pBM 10058, and Brooklyn Museum 37.1784Ea-b) is one of the best known examples of ancient Egyptian mathematics.
Plimpton 322 is a Babylonian clay tablet, believed to have been written around 1800 BC, that contains a mathematical table written in cuneiform script.
Archimedes of Syracuse (AR-kih-MEE-deez; around 287 – around 212 BC) was an Ancient Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor from the city of Syracuse in Sicily.
Pythagoras of Samos (around 570 – around 495 BC) was an ancient Ionian Greek philosopher, polymath, and the eponymous founder of Pythagoreanism.
Euclid (active 300 BC) was an ancient Greek mathematician active as a geometer and logician.

Hypatia (born around 350–370 – March 415 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher, astronomer, and mathematician who lived in Alexandria, at that time in the province of Egypt and a major city of the Roman Empire.

Brahmagupta (around 598 – around 668 AD) was an Indian mathematician and astronomer who is credited as the first person to understand and formalize the concept of the number zero for nothing in mathematics.
Aryabhata or Aryabhata I (476–550 AD) was the first of the major mathematician-astronomers and early physicist from the classical age of Indian mathematics and Indian astronomy.

Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, or simply al-Khwarizmi (around 780 – around 850) was a mathematician active during the Islamic Golden Age, who produced Arabic-language works in mathematics, astronomy, and geography.
Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.

Leonardo Bonacci, also Leonardo da Pisa (around 1170 – around 1240-50), commonly known as Fibonacci, was an Italian mathematician from the Republic of Pisa, considered to be "the most talented Western mathematician of the Middle Ages".

Pierre de Fermat (17 August 1601 – 12 January 1665) was a French magistrate, polymath, and mathematician credited for early developments that led to infinitesimal calculus, including his technique of adequality.
Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 – 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (or Leibnitz; 1 July 1646 [O.
In the history of calculus, the calculus controversy was a priority dispute between mathematicians Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz over who had first invented calculus.
Leonhard Euler (15 April 1707 – 18 September 1783) was a Swiss polymath who was active as a mathematician, physicist, astronomer, logician, geographer, music theorist and engineer.

Johann Carl Friedrich Gauss (30 April 1777 – 23 February 1855) was a German polymath active as a mathematician, astronomer, geodesist, and physicist, who contributed to many fields in mathematics and science.
Marie-Sophie Germain (1 April 1776 – 27 June 1831) was a French mathematician, physicist, and philosopher.
Évariste Galois (25 October 1811 – 31 May 1832) was a French mathematician and political activist.
Georg Ferdinand Ludwig Philipp Cantor (KAN-tor; 3 March [O.
David Hilbert (23 January 1862 – 14 February 1943) was a German mathematician and philosopher of mathematics.
Amalie Emmy Noether (23 March 1882 – 14 April 1935) was a German mathematician who made many important contributions to abstract algebra and mathematical physics.
Srinivasa Ramanujan Iyengar (22 December 1887 – 26 April 1920) was an Indian mathematician who worked during the early 20th century.
Kurt Friedrich Gödel (April 28, 1906 – January 14, 1978) was a logician, mathematician, cosmologist, and philosopher.
John von Neumann (December 28, 1903 – February 8, 1957) was a Hungarian and American mathematician, physicist, computer scientist and engineer.
Maryam Mirzakhani (12 May 1977 – 14 July 2017) was an Iranian mathematician and a professor of mathematics at Stanford University.
Mary Somerville (née Fairfax, formerly Greig; 1780–1872) was a Scottish scientist, writer, and polymath.

In mathematics, the notion of a number has been extended over the centuries to include zero (0), negative numbers such as negative one (minus 1), rational numbers such as one half open bracket, one ha

A numeral system is a writing system for expressing numbers without words; that is, a mathematical notation for representing numbers of a given set, using digits (in positional notation) or other symbols (in sign-value notation) in a consistent manner.
Counting refers to two interrelated processes: "Counting [something]" refers to determining how many elements there are in a finite set.
Tally marks, also called hash marks, are used as a basic numeral system for counting; they can be thought of as a unary numeral system.

An abacus (pl. abaci or abacuses), also called a counting frame, is a hand-operated calculating tool which was used from ancient times, in the ancient Near East, Europe, China, and Russia, until large
Roman numerals are a numeral system that originated in ancient Rome and remained the usual way of writing numbers throughout Europe well into the Late Middle Ages.
The Hindu–Arabic numeral system (also known as the Indo-Arabic numeral system, Hindu numeral system, and Arabic numeral system) is a base ten (decimal) positional numeral system.

Positional notation, also known as place-value notation, is the property of a numeral system that the value represented by each symbol in a written numeral depends not only on its appearance but also on its position.
0 (zero,) is a number representing an empty quantity.
In mathematics, a negative number is the opposite of a positive real number.
A fraction (from Latin: fractus, "broken") represents a part of a whole or, more generally, any number of equal parts.
A decimal system (also called base-ten, denary or decenary) is a numeral system that uses ten as its radix (base).
In mathematics, a percentage, percent, or per cent (from Latin per centum 'by a hundred') is a number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100.
In mathematics, a ratio shows how many times one number contains another.
In mathematics, the natural numbers are the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on, possibly excluding 0.

An integer is the number zero (0), a positive natural number (1, 2, 3,...), or the negation of a positive natural number (minus 1, minus 2, minus 3,...) The negations or additive inverses of the positive natural numbers are referred to as negative integers.
In mathematics, a rational number is a number that can be expressed as the quotient or fraction p over q of two integers, a numerator p and a nonzero denominator q.
In mathematics, the irrational numbers are all the real numbers that are not rational numbers; that is, irrational numbers are those that cannot be expressed as the ratio of two integers.
In mathematics, a real number is a number that can be used to measure a continuous one-dimensional quantity such as a length, duration or temperature.
An imaginary number is the product of a real number and the imaginary unit i, which is defined by its property i squared equals minus 1.

A binary number is a number expressed in the base-2 numeral system or binary numeral system, a method for representing numbers that uses only two symbols for the natural numbers: typically 0 (zero) and 1 (one).
Large numbers are numbers far larger than those encountered in everyday life, such as simple counting or financial transactions.
Arithmetic is an elementary branch of mathematics that deals with numerical operations like addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
Addition, usually denoted with the plus sign +, is one of the four basic operations of arithmetic, the other three being subtraction, multiplication, and division.
Subtraction (which is signified by the minus sign, −) is one of the four arithmetic operations along with addition, multiplication and division.
Multiplication is one of the four elementary mathematical operations of arithmetic, with the other ones being addition, subtraction, and division.
Division is one of the four basic operations of arithmetic.
In mathematics, a multiplication table (sometimes, less formally, a times table) is a mathematical table used to define a multiplication operation for an algebraic system.

Mental calculation (also known as mental computation) consists of arithmetical calculations made by the mind, within the brain, with no help from any supplies (such as pencil and paper) or devices such as a calculator.
Estimation (or estimating) is the process of finding an estimate or approximation, which is a value that is usable for some purpose even if input data may be incomplete, uncertain, or unstable.
In a ratio scale based on powers of ten, the order of magnitude is a measure of the nearness of two figures.
Adding the decimal digits of a positive whole number, while optionally ignoring any 9s or digits which sum to 9 or a multiple of 9.

In psychology, number sense is the term used for the hypothesis that some animals, particularly humans, have a biologically determined ability that allows them to represent and manipulate large numerical quantities.

In mathematics and computer programming, the order of operations is a collection of conventions about which arithmetic operations to perform first in order to evaluate a given mathematical expression.

In mathematics, brackets of various typographical forms, such as parentheses, square brackets [ ], braces open curly brace, close curly brace and angle brackets, are frequently used in mathematical notation.
In mathematics, the distributive property of binary operations is a generalization of the distributive law, which asserts that the equality
In mathematics, an interval is the set of all real numbers lying between two fixed lower or upper bounds ("endpoints" or boundary points) with no "gaps".
Algebra is a branch of mathematics that deals with abstract systems, known as algebraic structures, and the manipulation of expressions within those systems.
Elementary algebra, also known as high school algebra or college algebra, encompasses the basic concepts of algebra.
In mathematics, a variable (from Latin variabilis 'changeable') is a symbol, typically a letter, that refers to an unspecified mathematical object.
In mathematics, an equation is a mathematical formula that expresses the equality of two expressions, by connecting them with the equals sign =.
In mathematics, a linear equation is an equation that may be put in the form
In mathematics, a system of linear equations (or linear system) is a collection of two or more linear equations involving the same variables.
In mathematics, a quadratic equation (from Latin quadratus 'square') is an equation that can be rearranged in standard form as
In mathematics, a function from a set capital X to a set capital Y assigns to each element of capital X exactly one element of capital Y.
In mathematics, the graph of a function f is the set of ordered pairs open bracket, x, y, close bracket, where f of x equals y.

In geometry, a Cartesian coordinate system in a plane is a coordinate system that specifies each point uniquely by a pair of real numbers called coordinates, which are the signed distances to the poin

In mathematics, a polynomial is a mathematical expression consisting of indeterminates (also called variables) and coefficients, that involves only the operations of addition, subtraction, multiplicat
In mathematics, exponentiation, denoted b n, is an operation involving two numbers: the base, b, and the exponent, n.
In mathematics, the logarithm of a number is the exponent by which another fixed value, the base, must be raised to produce that number.
Exponential growth occurs when a quantity grows as an exponential function of time.
In mathematics, an inequality is a relation which makes a non-equal comparison between two numbers or other mathematical expressions.
In mathematics, the slope or gradient of a line is a number that describes the direction of the line on a plane.

In mathematics, factorization (or factorisation, see English spelling differences) or factoring consists of writing a number or another mathematical object as a product of several factors, usually smaller or simpler objects of the same kind.
Geometry is a branch of mathematics concerned with properties of space such as the distance, shape, size, and relative position of figures.
Euclidean geometry is a mathematical system attributed to Euclid, an ancient Greek mathematician, which he described in his textbook on geometry, Elements.
In mathematics, the Pythagorean theorem or Pythagoras's theorem is a fundamental relation in Euclidean geometry between the three sides of a right triangle.
A triangle or trigon is a polygon consisting of three sides connected at three corners.
A circle is a shape consisting of all points in a plane that are at a given distance from a given point, the centre.
In geometry, an angle is formed by two lines that meet at a point.
In geometry, a polygon is a plane figure made up of line segments connected to form a closed polygonal chain.
Area is the measure of a region's size on a surface.
Volume is a measure of regions in three-dimensional space.
Trigonometry is a branch of mathematics concerned with relationships between angles and side lengths of triangles.
In mathematics, sine and cosine are trigonometric functions.
In mathematics, non-Euclidean geometry consists of two geometries based on axioms closely related to those that specify Euclidean geometry.
In geometry, a Platonic solid is a convex, regular polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space.
In mathematics, two quantities are in the golden ratio if their ratio is the same as the ratio of their sum to the larger of the two quantities.

Topology is the branch of mathematics concerned with the properties of a geometric object that are preserved under continuous deformations, such as stretching, twisting, crumpling, and bending; that i
In mathematics, a Möbius strip, Möbius band, or Möbius loop is a surface that can be formed by attaching the ends of a strip of paper together with a half-twist.
In mathematics, a fractal is a geometric shape containing detailed structure at arbitrarily small scales, usually having a fractal dimension strictly exceeding the topological dimension.
A tessellation or tiling is the covering of a surface, often a plane, using one or more geometric shapes, called tiles, with no overlaps and no gaps.
Spherical geometry or spherics is the geometry of the two-dimensional surface of a sphere or the n-dimensional surface of higher dimensional spheres.
Logic is the study of correct reasoning.
Mathematical logic is the study of logic within mathematics.

In mathematics, a set is a collection of different things; the things are called elements or members of the set and are typically mathematical objects: numbers, symbols, points in space, lines, other geometric shapes, variables, functions, or even other sets.
Set theory is the branch of mathematical logic that studies sets, which can be informally described as collections of unique objects.
Naive set theory is any of several set theories used in the discussion of the foundations of mathematics.
A mathematical proof is a deductive argument for a mathematical statement, showing that the stated assumptions logically guarantee the conclusion.

In logic, reductio ad absurdum (Latin for "reduction to absurdity"), also known as argumentum ad absurdum (Latin for "argument to absurdity"), apagogical argument, or proof by contradiction, is the fo
Mathematical induction is a method for proving that a statement P of n is true for every natural number n, that is, that the infinitely many cases P of 0, P of 1, P of 2, P of 3, and so on all hold.
A syllogism is a kind of logical argument that applies deductive reasoning to arrive at a conclusion based on two propositions that are asserted or assumed to be true.
In mathematics and mathematical logic, Boolean algebra is a branch of algebra.
The square root of 2 (approximately 1.4142) is the positive real number that, when multiplied by itself or squared, equals the number 2.
An axiom, postulate, or assumption, is a statement that is taken to be true, to serve as a premise or starting point for further reasoning and arguments.
In mathematical logic, Russell's paradox (also known as Russell's antinomy) is a set-theoretic paradox published by the British philosopher and mathematician, Bertrand Russell, in 1901.
In philosophy and logic, the classical liar paradox or liar's paradox or antinomy of the liar is the statement of a liar that they are lying: for instance, declaring that "I am lying".
Probability concerns events and numerical descriptions of how likely they are to occur.
Probability theory or probability calculus is the branch of mathematics concerned with probability.
Statistics (from German: Statistik, orig.
In mathematics, an average of a collection or group is a value that is most central, common, or typical in some sense, and represents its overall position.
The median of a set of numbers is the value separating the higher half from the lower half of a data sample, a population, or a probability distribution.
In statistics, the standard deviation is a measure of the amount of variation of the values of a variable about its (arithmetic) average.
In probability theory and statistics, a normal distribution or Gaussian distribution is a type of continuous probability distribution for a real-valued random variable.

In probability theory, the law of large numbers is a mathematical law which states that the average of the results obtained from a large number of independent random samples converges to the true value, if it exists.

The gambler's fallacy, also known as the Monte Carlo fallacy or the fallacy of the maturity of chances, is the belief that an independent and equally probable outcome which happened less frequently th
The Monty Hall problem is a brain teaser, in the form of a probability puzzle, based nominally on the American television game show Let's Make a Deal and named after its original host, Monty Hall.
In probability theory, the birthday problem asks for the probability that, in a set of n randomly chosen people, at least two will share the same birthday.

In probability theory, Bayes' theorem (alternatively Bayes' law or Bayes' rule), named after Thomas Bayes, gives a mathematical rule for inverting conditional probabilities, allowing the probability of a cause to be found given its effect.

In statistics, regression toward the mean (also called regression to the mean, reversion to the mean, and reversion to mediocrity) is the phenomenon where if one sample of a random variable is extreme
Simpson's paradox is a phenomenon in probability and statistics in which a trend appears in several groups of data but disappears or reverses when the groups are combined.

The phrase "correlation does not imply causation" refers to the inability to legitimately deduce a cause-and-effect relationship between two events or variables solely on the basis of an observed association or correlation between them.
In common usage, randomness is the apparent or actual lack of definite patterns or predictability in information.
In probability theory, the expected value (also called expectation, mean, or first moment) is a generalization of the weighted average.

In probability theory, the central limit theorem (CLT) states that, under appropriate conditions, the distribution of a normalized version of the sample mean converges to a standard normal distribution.
Infinity is something which is boundless, limitless, or endless.

articles.t: Hilbert's paradox of the Grand Hotel
k: Hilbert's paradox of the Grand Hotel (colloquially the Infinite Hotel Paradox or Hilbert's Hotel) is a thought experiment which illustrates a counterintuitive property of infinite sets.

Zeno's paradoxes are a series of philosophical arguments presented by the ancient Greek philosopher Zeno of Elea (around 490–430 BC), primarily known through the works of Plato, Aristotle, and later commentators like Simplicius of Cilicia.
A prime number (or a prime) is a natural number greater than 1 that is not a product of two smaller natural numbers.
The number pi (spelled out as pi) is a mathematical constant, approximately equal to 3.14159, that is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
The number e is a mathematical constant that is the base of the natural logarithm and exponential function.
In mathematics, Euler's identity (also known as Euler's equation) is the equality
Chaos theory is a branch of mathematics and an interdisciplinary area of scientific study.

In chaos theory, the butterfly effect is the sensitive dependence on initial conditions in which a small change in one state of a deterministic nonlinear system can result in large differences in a later state.
Game theory is the field of applied mathematics that models strategic interactions between rational agents as "games" between "players".

In game theory, the prisoner's dilemma is a thought experiment involving two rational agents, each of whom can either cooperate for mutual benefit or betray their partner ("defect") for individual gain.
In mathematics, the Fibonacci sequence is a sequence in which each element is the sum of the two elements that precede it.

In mathematics, the four color theorem, or the four-color map theorem, states that no more than four colors are required to color the regions of any map so that no two adjacent regions have the same color.
In mathematics, the Riemann hypothesis asserts that the Riemann zeta function has its zeros only at the negative even integers and at complex numbers with real part one half.
The P versus NP problem is a major unsolved problem in theoretical computer science.
The Millennium Prize Problems are seven well-known complex mathematical problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000.
The Collatz conjecture is one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics.
Goldbach's conjecture is one of the oldest and best-known unsolved problems in number theory and all of mathematics.

The Seven Bridges of Königsberg is a historical puzzle asking for a walking tour through the bridges of the city of Königsberg (now Kaliningrad) where each of the city's bridges is crossed exactly once.
In mathematics and computer science, graph theory is the study of graphs, which are mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects.

Cantor's diagonal argument (among various similar names) is a mathematical proof that there are infinite sets which cannot be put into one-to-one correspondence with the infinite set of natural number

In computability theory, the halting problem is the decision problem of, given an arbitrary computer program and an input, determining whether said program will eventually finish running and halt, or will continue to run forever.

Benford's law, also known as the Newcomb–Benford law, the law of anomalous numbers, or the first-digit law, is an observation that in many real-life sets of numerical data, the leading digit is likely to be small.
The Mandelbrot set is a two-dimensional set.
Calculus is the branch of mathematics that studies continuous change, and is the principal precursor of modern mathematical analysis.
In mathematics, a limit is the value that a function (or sequence) approaches as the argument (or index) approaches some value.
In mathematics, the derivative is a fundamental tool that quantifies the sensitivity to change of a function's output with respect to its input.
In mathematics, an integral is the continuous analog of a sum, and is used to calculate areas, volumes, and their generalizations.

The fundamental theorem of calculus is a theorem that links the concept of differentiating a function (calculating its slopes, or rate of change at every point on its domain) with the concept of integ
In mathematics, a differential equation is an equation that relates one or more unknown functions and their derivatives.
In mathematics, an infinitesimal number is a non-zero quantity that is closer to 0 than any non-zero real number is.
The method of exhaustion is a method of finding the area of a shape by inscribing inside it a sequence of polygons (one at a time) whose areas converge to the area of the containing shape.

In calculus, Leibniz's notation, named in honor of the 17th-century German philosopher and mathematician Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, uses the symbols d x and d y to represent infinitely small (or infin
In mathematics, differential calculus is a subfield of calculus that studies the rates at which quantities change.
A quantity is subject to exponential decay if it decreases at a rate proportional to its current value.

A Malthusian growth model, sometimes called a simple exponential growth model, is essentially exponential growth based on the idea of the function being proportional to the speed to which the function grows.
In physics and mathematics, a brachistochrone curve, or curve of fastest descent, is the one lying on the plane between a point A and a lower point B, where B is not directly below A, on which a bead
In mathematical analysis, the Taylor series or Taylor expansion of a function is an infinite sum of terms that are expressed in terms of the function's derivatives at a single point.
